title: Deadlocks: Detection, Prevention, and Lock Ordering
lesson:
A deadlock happens when two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs and none can proceed. Classic example: transaction A updates row 1 then wants row 2, while transaction B has already updated row 2 and wants row 1. Both wait forever unless something intervenes. Deadlocks need four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait. Breaking any one of them removes the possibility.

Most relational databases do not prevent deadlocks; they detect them. The engine maintains a wait-for graph (transaction A waits for B, B waits for A) and periodically, or on each blocked lock request, looks for cycles. When it finds one, it picks a victim, often the transaction that has done the least work, rolls it back, and returns a deadlock error to that client. Some systems instead rely on a lock-wait timeout, which is simpler but slower to react and can abort transactions that were merely waiting behind a slow holder.

The most effective application-level prevention is a consistent lock ordering: if every code path acquires locks in the same global order (for example, always the lower account ID first), a circular wait cannot form. Other mitigations include keeping transactions short, touching rows in a deterministic order, avoiding user interaction while holding locks, and acquiring all needed locks up front with a single statement such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over the full set.

Because the database may abort any transaction at any time to break a cycle, clients must treat a deadlock error as retriable: re-run the whole transaction, ideally with a small randomized backoff. The retried transaction must be safe to repeat, which ties back to idempotency. In distributed settings spanning several nodes, per-node detectors cannot see the global graph, so systems typically fall back on timeouts or wound-wait and wait-die schemes that use transaction timestamps to decide who may wait.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the most effective application-level way to prevent deadlocks between transactions that lock multiple rows?
options: Acquiring locks in the same global order in every code path
Running every transaction at a lower isolation level
Holding locks for longer so work finishes in one go
questions.explanation: A consistent global lock order makes a circular wait impossible, which removes one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock.

questions.prompt: When a database detects a deadlock, it typically aborts one of the involved transactions and expects the client to retry it.
questions.explanation: The engine breaks the cycle by rolling back a victim transaction, so applications must handle the deadlock error and re-run the transaction.

questions.prompt: Databases detect deadlocks by searching for a cycle in the ____ graph.
questions.explanation: The wait-for graph has an edge from each transaction to the one whose lock it is waiting on, and a cycle means deadlock.

questions.prompt: Order the events in a two-transaction deadlock that the database resolves, earliest first.
items: The database rolls back one transaction as the victim
Each transaction requests the lock held by the other
Transaction A and B each acquire one lock
The surviving transaction acquires its lock and commits
The detector finds a cycle in the wait-for graph
questions.explanation: Locks are taken, each side then blocks on the other, the cycle is detected, a victim is rolled back, and the survivor can then proceed.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the four conditions required for a deadlock?
questions.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; eventual consistency is unrelated.
